This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $k\geq 2$ and define $n_k\geq 2k$ to be the least value of $n$ such that $n-i$ divides $\binom{n}{k}$ for all but one $0\leq i<k$. Estimate $n_k$.
#1063: [ErSe83]
number theory
A problem of Erdős and Selfridge posed in [ErSe83]. Erdős and Selfridge noted (and a proof can be found in [Mo85]) that if $n\geq 2k$ then there must exist at least one $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ does not divide $\binom{n}{k}$. 
We have $n_2=4$, $n_3=6$, $n_4=9$, and $n_5=12$. Monier [Mo85] observed that $n_k\leq k!$ for $k\geq 3$, since $\binom{k!}{k}$ is divisible by $k!-i$ for $1\leq i<k$. Cambie observes in the comments that this can be improved to\[n_k\leq k[2,3,\ldots,k-1]\leq e^{(1+o(1))k},\]where $[\cdots]$ is the least common multiple.
This is discussed in problem B31 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
Additional thanks to: Stijn Cambie

 Extending the computation to k = 75: 16 new terms, each verified minimal.
Taking rickyc's two results above as a *search accelerator* (the unique failing
index satisfies e = n mod k, and for each p^a || k,
p^(a + v_p(C(k-1,e)) + floor(log_p max(e, k-1-e))) divides n - e), every solution
with failing index r lies on the single progression n = r mod D(k,r), where D(k,r)
is the product of those prime powers. Sweeping all k such progressions below a
candidate is therefore exhaustive rather than heuristic. That extends OEIS
A389360, whose b-file ends at k = 59, by 16 terms:
 k n_k k n_k

 63 216949362182 71 13760436550

Each is minimal, not merely a solution: the sweeps below them tested
89,015,468,839 candidates in total with zero hits. As an arithmetic check on
coverage, the candidate count predicted independently from sum_r floor(n_k/D(k,r))
is 89,015,469,493, agreeing with the number actually enumerated to 7 parts in 10^9
(the difference is the n >= 2k floor). Positive control: the identical code path
re-derives all 58 published terms k = 2..59 with zero mismatches -- it found two
real bugs in the process (taking the first hit in r-order rather than the minimum
over r, and omitting the n >= 2k floor). Separately, a verifier sharing no code
with the searcher builds C(n,k) as an exact integer (451 to 905 decimal digits)
and tests divisibility straight from the definition: for all 16 terms there is
exactly one failing divisor, always at index n mod k.
Code, receipts and reproduction instructions:
https://github.com/Jaybell31/dreamwalk/tree/master/erdos1063
On StijnC's question of what estimate one should expect here, the extra terms say
the following.
(1) No new extreme in 38 further terms. n_k^(1/k) stays inside the band observed
for k <= 37: over 2 <= k <= 75 the maximum is still k = 10 (2.1781) and the
minimum still k = 31 (1.3368). The new terms only span 1.3658 (k = 67) to 1.6048
(k = 60).
(2) The prime/composite separation sharpens rather than washing out. Mean of
log(n_k)/k:
 k range primes composites
 2-19 0.4954 0.5825
 20-39 0.3390 0.5122
 40-59 0.3521 0.4502
 60-75 0.3264 0.4105
Regressing log(n_k)/k on k over k >= 20 gives slope -0.0026 for composite k but
-0.0002 for prime k. The apparent decay lives almost entirely on the composite
branch; the prime branch is close to flat near 0.33 across 55 terms. If the truth
is c^((1+o(1))k), these data are consistent with two different constants for the
two branches rather than one.
(3) The lower bound is still very far from the truth in this range:
n_k / LB(k) runs from 1.3e6 (k = 64) to 6.4e8 (k = 75), i.e. log(LB(k))/k is
roughly 0.07 to 0.23 against log(n_k)/k of roughly 0.31 to 0.47.
This does not resolve #1063 and claims no new theorem. The structural results are
rickyc's; they are used here but not re-proved formally, so minimality is
conditional on them (it is verified empirically on all 58 published terms as well
as the 16 new ones -- a Lean formalisation of the divisibility result would close
that gap). Machine arithmetic is u64; all values are below 2^63 and D(k,r)
overflow is detected rather than silently wrapped.

were produced with AI assistance (Claude, running in an agent harness). The claims
are computational and machine-checkable -- both implementations and the positive
control are in the linked repository and can be re-run in a few minutes.

 We prove the following lower bound:\[
n_k\ge 
\max\left(2k,\ \prod_{p^a\parallel k}p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k/2)\rfloor}\right).
\]Let \(n=n_k\), \(C=\binom nk\), and write \(d_i=n-i\). Let \(e\) be the unique index for which \(d_e\nmid C\). Fix \(p^a\parallel k\), and put\[
M=\max_{0\le i<k}v_p(d_i),\qquad S=v_p(C).
\]Since\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}v_p(d_i)-v_p(k!),
\]and the levels \(p,p^2,\ldots,p^a\) cancel exactly between the \(k\) consecutive integers \(d_i\) and \(k!\), while each higher level contributes at most \(1\), we have\[
S\le M-a.
\]Hence every \(d_i\) with \(v_p(d_i)=M\) fails to divide \(C\). Since there is only one failure, this maximum must occur at \(d_e\).
Now let\[
t=\lfloor\log_p(k/2)\rfloor .
\]Because \(p^t\le k/2\), among the \(k\) consecutive integers \(d_i\) at least two are divisible by \(p^t\). One may be \(d_e\), but another one divides \(C\), so \(S\ge t\). Therefore\[
M\ge a+t.
\]Thus\[
p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k/2)\rfloor}\mid d_e
\]for every \(p^a\parallel k\). Multiplying over \(p\mid k\) gives\[
\prod_{p^a\parallel k}p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k/2)\rfloor}\mid d_e\le n,
\]and since also \(n\ge2k\), the claimed lower bound follows. I am unsure whether this, combined with Stijn’s upper bound, resolves the problem. I do not think it does, since I would guess Erdős is asking for sharper bounds. (Note: This was AI assisted by GPT-5.5 Thinking)

 The same argument gives the stronger lower bound\[
n_k\ge
\max\left(2k,\ \prod_{p^a\parallel k}p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k-1)\rfloor}\right).
\]Keep the notation above. Since \(d_e\) is the unique term with \(v_p(d_e)=M\), for \(i\ne e\) we have\[
v_p(d_i)=v_p(d_i-d_e)=v_p(i-e).
\]Therefore\[
S=M+v_p(e!)+v_p((k-1-e)!)-v_p(k!)
=M-a-v_p\binom{k-1}{e}.
\]Hence\[
M=a+S+v_p\binom{k-1}{e}.
\]Now let\[
t=\lfloor\log_p(k-1)\rfloor,\qquad
r=\max(e,k-1-e),\qquad
u=\lfloor\log_p r\rfloor.
\]There is some \(i\ne e\) with \(|i-e|=p^u\). Since \(d_i\mid C\), we have \(S\ge u\). Also \(r\ge(k-1)/2\), so \(u\ge t-1\). If \(u=t-1\), then\[
e,\ k-1-e<p^t\le k-1,
\]so their addition has a carry in base \(p\), and hence by Kummer's theorem\[
v_p\binom{k-1}{e}\ge1.
\]Thus in either case\[
S+v_p\binom{k-1}{e}\ge t,
\]and therefore\[
M\ge a+t.
\]Thus\[
p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k-1)\rfloor}\mid d_e
\]for every \(p^a\parallel k\). Multiplying over \(p\mid k\) gives\[
\prod_{p^a\parallel k}p^{a+\lfloor\log_p(k-1)\rfloor}\mid d_e\le n,
\]and again since \(n\ge2k\), the claimed lower bound follows. I still do not think this resolves the problem, as the gap between the lower and upper bound remains large. (Note: This comment was written by GPT-5.6 Sol)

 Small observation related to the one by Monier:
$n_k\le k \cdot lcm( \{2,3,\ldots,k-1\})$ by the same reason for $k \ge 3$.
This implies an exponential upper bound $\exp((1+o(1))n).$

Hereby it is not sure if it is of the form $c^{(1+o(1))n}$ for some constant $c$, or there is an exponential lower- and upper-bound of the latter form, but $1/k \log n_k$ does not converge.
